utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we resume the examination of the witness, Mr. Hannis, could you please inform the Chamber about the position the Defence globally takes in respect of the translation, interpretation issue raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution's global position is that we oppose the motion. We have a concern about the amount of resources it would require. We think that although it may not result in a perfect trial for the defendant, it will result in a fair trial for him having audios of, for example, the transcripts of testimony in this case and the transcripts from the other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you would like to do it right away, Mr. Stewart, or let's say just before the break. You have made reference in your motion to the Luedicke case and to the Artico case. And the Chamber is still wondering to what extent the factual situation in these cases, apart from general statements in the decisions, would be comparable to the present situation, and the same would, by the way, be true for the Kamasinski case as well, which is a case later than the Luedicke case and refers to the Luedicke case, but very specifically enters the issue of translations and interpretations. I don't know whether it was just a general reference to general statements in these cases or that the factual situations in these cases would in your view support the present motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. The -- may I say straight away, Your Honour, by the way just to introduce a new member of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mieke Dixon, on my far left. The other faces I think are pretty familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not her birthday by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was very recently, Your Honour. But she hasn't got another one for nearly a year now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of fact, we didn't consider that the facts of those cases were at all close, but of course they're there for anybody to look at, and naturally we can show them to Your Honour to make that point. So it was certainly not that the factual context of those cases was supportive, it actually made them -- in our submission makes them really irrelevant as far as the particular application of the facts in those cases are concerned, but the principles are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Artico case as far as I know is a counsel which is I would say almost completely passive, doing nothing, and of course this Chamber could not understand any relation to that case. The Luedicke case mainly dealing with translation during trial and especially imposing upon the accused the costs of that, whereas the Kamasinski case came far closer to, as far as the issues are concerned, the issues being to what extent an accused is entitled to receive translations, not only of the trial proceedings during trial but also of supporting material, indictment, et cetera. But I do understand that the facts of these cases did not -- are not specifically relied upon by the Defence. The Chamber will consider whether to give a decision before the recess, which might have some advantages, at least it leaves the Defence not for a very long time in uncertainty. But we'll have to consider that first. If we would give a decision, it would be an oral decision because we find no time before tomorrow morning to write it down in sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say that -- I haven't come equipped this very second to deal with this motion at all, as I'm sure Your Honours would appreciate. I haven't even brought a copy of it with me into Court right now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I would be very passive as far as that's concerned, for the immediate future, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just wonder whether at some point whether it might be helpful - I want to check against the motion, and indicate to Your Honour perhaps what the Defence would regard as the most helpful points to have decided sooner rather than later because they're not all in the same category, they don't all have the same impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The most important category, being the transcripts of the hearings in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour has it then. That would be the most helpful of all to have decided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, Mr. Margetts. You indicated that you would play a video which would take approximately 15 minutes and then would have some additional questions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just have one preliminary matter with respect to translations, then there are three documents which will be quite quick. And then the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The preliminary matter is that I have now obtained revised translations of Exhibits P226.1 and Exhibit P230.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please assist me, these are the new ones? I haven't got it in my memory. The decision signed by Jovo Banjac would be number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P226.1. Then the joint official announcement of which Mr. -- signed also by Mr. Egrlic would then be P230.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we resume, Mr. Egrlic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. I take it that's clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Margetts, if there are no other -- are there any further preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No further preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, while you were in Manjaca, did you see any Serb politicians in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one visit by one Serb politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who was that politician?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you recall the position that he held?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a rather high place, maybe in the assembly or the Serb autonomous region. I can't recall exactly which position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When did he attend Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that he had to say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He went into every barn where prisoners were detained and talked to people, saying that the day when they would be free is coming soon, that the situation will be resolved very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Immediately following his visit, did anything change in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing changed. Everything remained exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have the next three exhibits marked and placed before the witness. The next exhibit is the document dated 29 January 1993 with the ERN Y0017553. Then the document dated 25 September 1992 with the ERN 01905109. And following that, the exhibit that appears in the list as dated 1st July 1992 which is marked 03008004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, they would have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document dated the 29th of January 1993 gets Exhibit Number P249 and its English translation gets Exhibit Number P249.1. The second document dated 25th of September 1992 gets Exhibit Number P250 and its English translation gets Exhibit Number P250.1. The third document dated July 1992 gets Exhibit Number P251 and its English translation gets Exhibit Number 251.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, could you please refer to the document with the list of names on it, and could you identify whether or not your name is on this list.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 36th place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I'll refer now to the next document. Mr. Egrlic, this is a document signed by Vinko Kondic, and it's dated 25 September 1992. And it details matters that according to Mr. Kondic took place in the Kljuc Municipality. Could I refer you to the second paragraph, and in particular, the second half of that paragraph, and the sentence that commences "the TO's main leaders were Asim Egrlic..." Mr. Egrlic, how do you respond to the characterisation of you as "the main leader of the alleged Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says one of the main leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the question must be more carefully put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you respond to being described here as "one of the main leaders," Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you refer to the "Territorial Defence," can you again inform the Court as to what the state of organisation of the Territorial Defence was.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the TO staff had been appointed. After a while, the whole staff was designated and was established to some extent. And its main activity was to organise those village guards that were supposed to evolve eventually into TO units; however, that did not happen because of the circumstances under which the staff was working, as the Kljuc Municipality had by that time been already taken over by the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished now with that document. If we could move to the next document, which is a report dated July 1992 headed: "Information on the work and activities of the Kljuc SJB." And again, this is a document that purports to be signed by Vinko Kondic. Mr. Egrlic, can I refer you to page 8 of that document, and in particular, the paragraph that appears under the heading, "Section VI, the course of armed operations." I'll just read that paragraph aloud and ask you to respond to this paragraph. It states that "Armed operations in the area of Kljuc Municipality began on 27 May 1992. On that day, Muslim extremists and fundamentalists carried out several synchronised armed operations against the police and the Serbian Army in an attempt to destroy the main body of the police force and the RSM and to force the withdrawal of our forces from the front line by attacking them, thus weakening our positions in the direction of Kupres, Jajce, and Bihac." Mr. Egrlic, is that a correct statement of the activities of any units on the 27th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to apologise but I didn't find this paragraph on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Egrlic. I meant to refer to page 8, and it's under the heading denoting section VI, and that appears at the bottom of page 8. Please take your time to read that paragraph and respond to any part of that paragraph informing the Court whether or not it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is stated in this paragraph is not correct because on that day it says here that the Muslim extremists and fundamentalists carried out a number of synchronised armed actions against members of the Serbian military police. There wasn't any action of any kind because the guards until then had worked at night started working during the day, and they were at their homes, in front of their thresholds. And the incident that occurred in an area where these people lived. They didn't go anywhere, and they didn't take any sort of action. They didn't attack anyone. They were at home when the Serbian police and the army came with the intention of disarming the citizens, entering their houses, et cetera. And this is how and where the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished with that document. I'd just like to ask you one further question and then show you some segments of a videotape. That question is this: When you returned to the Municipality of Kljuc in September 1995, did you attend any exhumation sites; and if so, could you detail those sites to the Court and inform the Court of what you observed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present when almost all the exhumations were performed since I was the presiding officer of the municipal council. But as a citizen, it was my duty to go to all exhumation sites in the territory of the Municipality of Kljuc. I was present and I went to two mass graves in Laniste, one was called Babina Dolina, and the other one was called Bezdana. That's a cave. And I went to the mass grave at Crvena Zemlja, the red earth, and then there was a mass grave in a valley in the village of Prhovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And upon your attendance at those sites, did you learn how many bodies were exhumed from those graves?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The mass grave at Laniste, as far as I can remember, there were about 188 bodies that were exhumed there. That's in a cave not far from the barracks where the Serbian Army was located. The second mass Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond grave was at the place called Babina Dolina. There were about 130 bodies exhumed there. In the first mass grave, there were the bodies of citizens from the local commune of Biljani, which is about 18 kilometres from that site. And in the second mass grave, the bodies of people from the Velagic local commune were found. In the Prhovo mass grave, about 45 bodies were exhumed, whereas in the Crvena Zemlja or Red Earth mass grave, about 30 bodies were exhumed as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people whose bodies were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I'd now like to show you segments of a videotape if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question on this point. Mr. Egrlic, could you tell us whether the exhumed Bosniak bodies, were they men, women? Do you know anything about age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were mostly men, but there were women and children, too. There were of different ages, between a few months old up until the age of about 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever learned the identity of those persons, those bodies exhumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost all of the bodies exhumed were identified and buried in the local communes that they had lived in. They were buried in the local cemeteries there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent that you have known these people, and first of all, did you know one or more, and if more, how many approximately of those persons whose bodies were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew some of them, some of them were my relatives or friends. I had known some of them for a long time, whereas there were others whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent known to you, do you know whether they were members of armed forces or otherwise involved in armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am aware, they weren't members of armed forces, and they didn't participate in conflicts of any kind. These people were taken out of their houses and shot at various locations, in Biljani near the school, and in Velagic they were shot in front of the old school. And in Prhovo, this was done in the immediate vicinity of the valley which is where they were subsequently buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to now present to the witness a transcript of a videotape that appears on the exhibit list marked with the date 1 July 1992, the ERN for the English is L0068783. We do not propose to play the entire video because it's in excess of half an hour. What we do propose to do is to play six segments of that video and ask the witness to comment on each of those segments. And the total time of those segments will be about 14 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the transcript would have -- let's first -- I take it that the video will be tendered as well. The video on CD-ROM will receive --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will have the Exhibit Number P252. The English transcript will have the Exhibit Number P252.A, and the B/C/S transcript will have the Exhibit Number P252.A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the original English or is the original B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The original is B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that the English translation gets 252.A.1, and the B/C/S version of the transcript gets P252.A. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first segment is the segment at the time markings 20 minutes 36 seconds to 21 minutes 23 seconds. And that segment could be played for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] In Kljuc, the Crisis Staff takes over the power. Many decisions have been passed, starting with the introduction of a curfew, then the termination of work in all enterprises, and in most institutions, which meant a transfer to typical wartime conditions of work and life. It was only in the last several days that the Crisis Staff issued an order that the citizens were allowed to move from 0700 up to 2000 hours, that the shops could be opened as well as restaurants and caterers from 7.00 to 8.00 p.m. with the restriction that alcohol could be served only until 1800. What is most important is that some decisions were passed regarding the commencement of production in some enterprises, primarily the largest Kljuc enterprise, SIP Kljuc. Annual service activities will begin there a month earlier than previously anticipated. As of 12th June, a regular bus line was established connecting Vrbljani with Kljuc and Banja Luka via Sitnica, Sljicic, and Han Kol. Buses will depart from Vrbljani at 5.30 and from Kljuc --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, what was depicted in the footage in that segment?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain parts of the town of Kljuc were depicted. It was possible to see the bus station, the commercial area, the business premises of Sipad enterprise, and it was possible to see the main street in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Does the commentary accompanying that footage accurately reflect what occurred in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the first part is concerned, as far as the crisis staff taking over power is concerned and with regard to the decisions to introduce a curfew, et cetera, I can confirm that this is right. But as to the buses and to their destinations, I know nothing about that because I was already in detention at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If the second segment could be played, and that is the segment from 22 minutes and 4 seconds to 28 minutes and 9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] "Negotiations have been held with the most extreme wing and the reply was that they did not wish civilian victims, but they wouldn't give up at any cost, and they would rather die in battle than give in their weapons. These are extremists I'm talking about, the wing that is so close and gives an accurate picture of what Muslim fundamentalism is about. This leader of the extremists, was he here? In the area of Kljuc Municipality, we proved it in our operations. We proved, we ascertained that there was a bond between the official leadership of the SDA and the Muslim Bosniak Party, the party, the organisation, and that the leaders of these parties were directly involved in supplying weapons, in establishing units, and that the whole process was organised and realised through political parties. Tell us what was going on when it was clear that they did not want to negotiate, that they would not hand over their weapons in a legal manner, that they wanted war? What did the other, Serbian side do, what did the police do? Well, we replied to such a challenge using our own violent method. We set deadlines for them to surrender, as an ultimatum, and after that we let them know explicitly that we would use combat means to destroy their manpower completely. We would not be responsible in that case for the civilians in the region of combat activities since there were cases we had been aware of at the time, that they had threatened their own population, and there are even cases in which they had shot at their own people not allowing them to leave and find shelter in some other locations. What villages are you referring to? The core, the focus of activities was the region of the villages of Pudin Han, Velagici, Gornji Ramici, Krasulje, and the area in the direction of Donja Sanica bordering with Sanski Most Municipality, the villages of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo that have for a long time had the reputation of the most powerful strongholds of Muslim fundamentalists. How many Muslims are there with permanent residence there? In this part of Kljuc Municipality, there were some 12.500 Muslims, and they make up over 70 per cent of the total Muslim population. I also would like to say that there are about 4.300 Serbs living in this area, and in all their options, this region should be included in the so-called Bosnian Municipality of Kljuc since the deputies of the SDA and MBO, they call themselves the Muslim National Bloc, proclaimed a Bosnian Muslim Municipality of Kljuc as early as in December. They were actually the first ones to do so in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was the result of the activities of your police force and the Serb Army, the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Actions were taken in an energetic way and in a very short period, in a period of just a few hours, the units had been broken down. Most of their members surrendered, either by handing over their personal weapons or they surrendered without weapons. A small number of them, some 20 to 30 per cent of the extremists withdrew in order to resume their activities in the region of the local Sanica community, and in the area of the Sanski Most Municipality where they can still be found in small groups. According to some information, some of them attempted to get to the Prijedor Municipality or the Municipality of Bihac. A great many houses have been pulled down. The population that used to reside here has fled. Many have been taken prisoners. A newly-built mosque has been destroyed, one that had not officially been opened yet. Still the Serbian military and police were targeting only houses from where resistance was coming. The new mosque in Velagic or in Pudin Han was used as one of the most powerful Muslim strongholds. The Muslims did not want to accept the peace offered by the Serbs, neither in Krasulje, nor in Gornja and Donja Sanica, Plemenica, Prhovo, Ramici, and Kamicka. Therefore, during the cleansing some of the houses in these villages were destroyed and some other facilities as well, but a lot less than in Velagici and Pudin Han. What happened to the other Muslim villages? Except for the part of the village where fortified facilities were established and ambushes laid by the members of the Muslim Territorial Defence and the Green Berets, in order to make themselves ready for combat activities, we did not perform any other activities. In the town of Kljuc itself, including the surrounding villages such as Sehici, Egrlici, Velecevo, Dubocanin, the Zgon settlement which were populated exclusively by Muslim people there was no destruction. In these regions not a single bullet was fired. First because in some parts of these settlements, it had not been possible to influence the Muslim population ideologically. This is the reason why we had no need to destroy places where there was no resistance."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, who was the person depicted in that footage?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person depicted was Vinko Kondic, the chief of the Kljuc police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In your previous testimony before this Court, you have detailed events that took place in the time period that Mr. Kondic is referring to, and your testimony can be compared with the details of what Mr. Kondic stated. But in general terms, how do you respond to Mr. Kondic's description of events?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as Mr. Kondic's comments are concerned, it is obvious that he made these comments in view of a certain scheme that they had. This was a programme that was shown in wartime conditions. So what we saw is a certain way of justifying what had been done in that area. The commentary states that the most extreme segment of the Bosniak Territorial Defence had been destroyed, but the commentary doesn't mention the fact that our villages were entered and that they killed the population and set fire to almost all the buildings the Bosniaks lived in at the time. It's obvious that this is a very biased depiction, the purpose of which is to encourage the combatants of the Republika Srpska Army and to demoralise the entire population in the area they lived in. Its purpose was to depict matters from their own point of view. They wanted to depict matters in a positive light. In my opinion, that is the objective of this commentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you agree or disagree with the depiction?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many things that were said here that I disagree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In the course of your previous answer, you quoted the video and stated that "the commentary states that the most extreme segment of the Bosniak Territorial Defence had been destroyed." Was there an extreme segment of the Bosniak Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no extreme segment, and a Territorial Defence as it has been referred to here did not exist. The fact that the entire population was considered as the Territorial Defence and that there were arrests and people were taken to school facilities and people were taken to Manjaca, this all attests to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The segment depicted a view from a car that was travelling along. Were you able to identify the area that was being filmed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the Pudin Han and Velagici settlements were shown. And it was possible to see some houses there which had been destroyed. And here, it states that the mosque was destroyed since fire was opened from that location. I don't know what the exact wording was. I won't look for it here. But they claim that the greatest extremists were located in that mosque. And that's quite simply a lie. This was just an excuse to destroy other mosques, too, because in the territory of the Municipality of Kljuc, 17 mosques were destroyed as well as one Catholic church. The pretext was the same in all of these cases. 3.500 houses were also destroyed, and the same excuse was given. Over 5.000 individuals were tortured and questioned, but it's not possible for women and children and toddlers to be members of the Territorial Defence. And about 1.300 people ended up in Manjaca. All of this was quite obviously calculated. These were lies, these were actions that led to the destruction, the annihilation of the Bosniaks in that area because later on the entire population was driven out, about 17.000 inhabitants were expelled from that area. And upon returning in 1995, only 600 individuals remained in the area, most of them only because they were unable to leave, and they lived there in extremely difficult conditions. They were humiliated on a daily basis and were forced to do labour. Some were forced to go to the lines to dig trenches there, and others were forced to sweep the streets and to clean the streets. That's how things were, and this has not been mentioned here. And if it were possible to find this situation depicted in such a manner in this wartime report, then we would have a more complete view of the situation. utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were any mosques standing in Kljuc when you returned to Kljuc in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had all been destroyed. All 17 mosques had been destroyed as well as a Catholic church. They had been razed to the ground. The town mosque had been cleared of debris, whereas the others were in a state of total disrepair. They were ruins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was the condition of your property when you returned to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hasn't the witness not already answered that question right in the beginning of his testimony just as the all 17 mosques being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, if that is Your Honours' recollection, I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness testified, and I'm quite sure that he found his house burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Let us move to the next segment. And that is the segment that appears at the counter marking 30 minutes 59 seconds to 31 minutes 41 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] In the course of combat activities in the area, the formations of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina arrived, and their units established full command and control over the territory in the region, and there were no combat activities, neither was there substantial firing going on. There were no attempts to take over this section. There was occasional fire opened by fanatics from the forests who didn't want" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you've previously given testimony in relation to these matters, so I don't intend you to ask you any questions about that segment. Let's move to the next segment which is the segment that appears at the counter reference 39 minutes 52 to 42 minutes 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] Although Filipovic knows very well, and we publicly state to his supporters to open their eyes and to open the eyes of all Muslims who follow him, a toast to his health, and Omer Filipovic heard this in prison somewhere because already on the 28th of May, only a day after the outbreak of the war in the area of Velagici and Pudin Han, he was led away by the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he has no clue of the alleged arrest of 4.000 Serbs. It is true that rather a lot of Muslim extremists were captured during the cleansing of Velagici, Pudin Han, Krasulje, Ramici, Crljeni, Kamicka, Plemenica, Prhovo and some other villages, and in the area of Kljuc. With Omer Filipovic complete lists of the composition of the crisis and war staff were found as well as of the military structure of the Green Berets in this area, attack and retreat plans, lists which people should be liquidated and how and where to get arms. Most of the members of their crisis staff have been arrested. They namely had a crisis staff and a war staff. The war staff was commanded by Omer Filipovic, coordinators in the field were Amir Avdic and Nevzad Djeric, and Asim Egrlic was responsible for political affairs. The first three are JNA reserve officers. Filipovic is a lieutenant. He was brought in as a commander and arrested together with Asim Egrlic, who had been wounded on the first day in the course of combat actions. He was brought in as well. The president of the Party of Democratic Action was brought in, the other is president of the MBO party. Avdic and Djeric are still on the run, and they constitute the harshest, most extreme part of the Green Berets in the Kljuc Municipality. The crisis staff was composed of a larger number of people. It consisted of Asim Egrlic, Omer Filipovic, Iksan Zukanovic, Suad Mesic, Ibrahim Egrlic, Muhamed Filipovic and a certain number of couriers and drivers which is not that important. Most of the crisis staff members have also been brought in and are being operatively processed so we will establish the individual part and responsibility of each of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, again, you have provided detailed testimony in relation to matters relevant to the statements of Mr. Kondic. But in general terms, and only in general terms, how do you respond to these comments of Mr. Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kondic wanted to present things in a certain light here. In his version, the Territorial Defence staff, or rather the majority of its members, were arrested and taken into custody, which was correct. And this was a way of boosting the morale of the Army of Republika Srpska so that they step up their activities in terms of arresting, rounding up people in the belief that this population was now left without their leaders and they could do with them what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could play the next segment, which is between the time markings 49 minutes 25 through to 50 minutes 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] We came across another one about whom Sarajevo TV claims that he is in another world for a long time already, it is Dr. Emir Kapetanovic. What I have to say is that I and my brother Nermin Kapetanovic and my family are safe and sound. Nobody from the authorities harassed us, nobody bothered us, arrested us, or summoned us to the police. Most likely because they had no reason to do so. Generally speaking, I have nothing else to say. I don't go to town much due to the circumstances. Every so often, I go out and play some ball, basketball. I socialise normally. How about the situation in the area of the hostilities? What happened to your shop? The shop, my practice, I'm a gynecologist by profession. My practice is out of town. I moved there through a combination of circumstances because I could not afford to pay for premises in town. You know how high the rents are there. I was in the zone of war and operations, and alas it was hit. The practice does not exist any more. The bottom line is a lot has been destroyed. They called me, told me later to go to the SUP to report the damage, which is normal as all other citizens. I hope that of course some can be bought, repaired, acquired from abroad, most likely at some other location when all calms down a bit. The current authorities, of course, know who was involved and what to do about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, does that footage depict Mr. Emir Kapetanovic, and what happened to Mr. Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this film, we see Dr. Emir Kapetanovic, who is shown standing at the football pitch near a primary school, in fact, a basketball pitch. And he was making this statement about the good life he was leading there without any problems. However, after making this statement, Dr. Kapetanovic was brought to the Manjaca camp where he was beaten up, a beating that he barely survived. Most of his time in Manjaca, he spent in the horseshed where he was found by the Doctors Without Borders who had come together with ICRC representatives, and they singled him out along with the most infirm and the most seriously ill and saved him from Manjaca. He currently lives somewhere in the United States. What we saw in that film was an attempt to show the way the new authorities were full of respect for human rights and international commitments, to make it seem that everything was already for Muslim citizens. They were even able to play basketball, which is a blatant lie because all that time Dr. Kapetanovic was at Manjaca. This was a simple propaganda tool, just as the entire television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When did Dr. Kapetanovic arrive at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived, if I remember correctly, in mid-July, maybe late June or mid-July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the basis of your knowledge as to the arrival date of Dr. Kapetanovic and your knowledge in relation to the other events depicted on this video, when was this video shot?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by what he said about most of the extremists having been taken into custody and arrested, the members of the Territorial Defence village by village as enumerated there, I think this video could have been made between the 20th of June and the 15th of July because that part coincides exactly with a number of people who were brought to Manjaca already at that time. They were already over 1.000 people from Kljuc in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I have a final segment of the video to show you, and I'll ask you for a brief comment on that. And that will be the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The timing references are between 53 minutes 59 and 56 minutes and 6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: COMMENTARY: [Voiceover] "The political and security situation in the Kljuc Municipality is quite complicated. We can say today that in the last ten days the situation has improved somewhat. One can say that the situation is calming down, life is coming back to normal, and business is picking up, and in future we will secure a normal life and business in the territory of the whole municipality provided that certain systems, public and economic institutions, start functioning as well. Let me ask you frankly, do you think that it is possible after all these events that Muslims and Serbs would live together in the area of your municipality? It is difficult to answer this question. I mean, how can one assess something like that. I think that life has to be totally ethnically separated and the areas ethnically cleansed of all those who cannot live together. Well, is this better done by war or by peaceful means? In my opinion, the only solution would be peaceful. Never by war. I think that we have not that much influence in small communities like Kljuc. I think that the leadership on the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have to do this job, and we will do what we can on that level and pass it on to the level of municipalities belonging to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. If I understood you correctly, this means it is up to Dr. Karadzic in the first place, the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to find a solution in talks with Alija Izetbegovic and with Boban? In this case, with Izetbegovic because it concerns the Muslims of your municipality. I think that this is the only possible solution. If this solution is not achieved soon, I am afraid that we will get into an even more difficult situation, because the war is not over yet. The war goes on and can easily turn into an war up to the extinction of one or the other side."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who was the speaker in that segment?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speaker was Jovo Banjac, president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In this depiction, he states, "I think that life has to be totally ethnically demarcated and the areas ethnically cleansed of all those who cannot live together in that area." He is asked: "Well, is this better done by war or peacefully?" He responds: "In my opinion, the only solution would be peaceful, never by war. I think that we have not much influence on this in small communities like Kljuc. I think that the leadership on the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have to do this job," and he continues. Was that consistent with comments Mr. Banjac made to you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That's all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you'll -- after a break, you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence. At this moment, you are excused for approximately 40 minutes. So we would like to see you back after that break. No, we're not yet, Mr. Usher. There was a request by the accused to address the Chamber for 10 to 15 minutes. That will be exactly the time until the next break. So therefore, we would like to give an opportunity to -- but perhaps you first escort the witness out of the courtroom. The Chamber prefers to use this moment, Mr. Krajisnik, to give you an opportunity to address us because if there would be anything that would need further thought, tomorrow being the last day before the recess, we would rather not wait until then. So the next 10 to 15 minutes are yours to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wish to thank you, Your Honours, for giving me this opportunity to address you briefly. I am aware that you have precious little time at your disposal, and that's why I'm even more thankful. I'll try to be as brief as possible. I did not intend to make a problem out of the decision that you have made. I am aware that the decision of the Trial Chamber is binding for me, and I respect that. I mean, the decision not to extend this trial, or rather, grant additional time for the preparation of the Defence case. I hope that my Defence team will continue to cooperate with you successfully and manage to adjust the time necessary. What I wanted to emphasise in relation to this decision as well: I wish to express my respect for the Trial Chamber because this trial is an opportunity for me to find the truth, and I wish to come back to that moment when you granted me leave to address you before the beginning of trial. I asked you then, although I had pled not guilty, I had asked you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond not to take me at my word, but just to help me bring the truth to light because nobody's more interested in the truth than I. Let me avail myself of this opportunity. After this decision refusing leave to use up additional time for preparing my Defence case, there was another problem. I respect my Defence team. I think Mr. Stewart is defending me very competently and very well. He told me that we have not yet mounted a good defence, we have not prepared ourselves sufficiently for defending Mr. Krajisnik. I am not going to give too many examples, but it is clear that witness testimony could have been economised and the time of the Trial Chamber could have been saved in proving certain things. What can be done now? I hope you will bear one thing in mind. In order to ensure a fair trial, I cannot really give any terribly wise advice on how my Defence team should get ready. How can we help my Defence team led by Mr. Stewart have the best preparation possible? You know that this can be done with my participation, and in that participation I'm rather handicapped. You saw on this example of translation of transcripts that I cannot always help much. The transcript would mean a lot to me if I can review what each of the witness's said. Of course, I can take notes, but that's not the same thing. Also, I don't have enough opportunity to have quality communication with my Defence because I don't speak English and they don't speak Serbian. Second, I don't receive the transcript. I can't receive it. And third, there are a lot of documents coming in from the OTP with B/C/S versions becoming available two or three days prior to being used. What has been my problem so far? For instance, I had a chance of contacting a lawyer at Pale in Republika Srpska. Through temporary telephone communications, due to lack of means, that lawyer will not be able to participate in my Defence, and I kindly ask you to allow me the use of privileged telephone communication to secure some other lawyer who could take part in my Defence. Another thing, if you ruled that I don't have the right to receive the transcript, could I then bring my computer here and take notes in the courtroom so as to be able to take to my prison cell the transcript that I created for my own purposes? And lastly, since you ruled as you ruled on my financial contribution to my Defence costs, there are two small requests concerning finances, and they are before the Registry. One that you have seen is my request for the Registry to vary their decision on my financial contribution. And the second is as follows: In the course of attempts to establish the truth, the Registry challenged certain documents because they looked as if they had been created later than the date on them. Since these documents were seized when I was arrested, we received confirmation from the OTP that these documents were available and were seized at the time of my arrest. And my request would be to review the possibilities for helping me to participate in my Defence because I'm the best witness in my Defence, if only I had a slightly better communication. And your help would also be appreciated in my dealings with the Registry, in getting them to approve me privileged telephone communications and in getting them to reverse their decision on my financial contribution. I don't know how things are developing in other trials, but I know that you are very attentive in my trial. Just one more thing: What looks like an attempt to adjust, to harmonise the positions between the Defence and OTP, please, put a stop to it. Please let the truth come to light. There are three truths here. One is the truth of Serbian witnesses; another is the truth of Muslim witnesses; and the third is in the middle. I am very surprised to see and hear many things I've seen here. Let this end there. I really want the real truth to be established, and I thank you for giving me this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Briefly, I'll respond to a few matters. The issue of privileged telephone conversations is primarily in the hands of the Registrar. The Registrar is responsible for detention facilities. If there ever is a decision taken by the Registrar which could have an impact upon the fairness of this trial, then there is an inherent power of the Trial Chamber to review that decision. That is not to put its own assessment of the situation in the place of the assessment made by the Registrar, but just a review on whether the decision of the Registrar would make the trial unfair. So the first step always to be taken is to address the Registrar. As far as the use of a computer in this courtroom is concerned, as such, the Trial Chamber is not inclined to make any difference on whether you use a fountain pen, a pencil, or a computer. However, computers are known to have sometimes an impact on security matters. If there is no such thing at hand, then the Chamber will certainly seriously consider to give you an opportunity to use a laptop computer here and to use your notes, then, in the Detention Unit. The written transcripts in a language you understand of this trial is the subject of a motion, as you are aware of, filed by the Defence. We heard a global position, a general position taken by the Prosecution this afternoon. And as I indicated before, the Chamber will consider whether or not still to give a decision before the recess. Then you referred in -- at different moments to the financial matters. You said that a lawyer in Pale could not assist you due to your lack of financial means. You also referred to the decision on the financial means to be varied by the Registrar. There, again, the first authority to be addressed is the Registrar, and the Chamber can only play a role after a decision is there and if the requirements are met for an involvement of the Chamber in the matter. Finally, you said something about documents that were created not -- or at least I did understand you to say that documents that were considered to have been anti-dated. If there were any new facts to be submitted in that respect, then again it is the first and the primary responsibility of the Registrar to deal with it, and only if all requirements are met the Chamber can be involved in that. Finally, you said something about the truth presented by the Serbian witnesses, truth presented by Muslim witnesses, and the in-between situation. The Chamber is not trying to achieve to a truth, but to the truth. We'll adjourn until a quarter past 4.00 when the Defence counsel may start the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart, or is it Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things very briefly, I wonder if Your Honour would give me, that's to say the Defence team, five minutes either immediately before or immediately after a break at some convenient point this afternoon so that the witness need not be here at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the motion filed or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's two things, Your Honour, briefly. One is in relation to my client's comments to the Court, and secondly, just one or two observations on that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give you five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either just before or after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged. I've got one other thing to say, Your Honour, which would be, in this particular instance, it would be more suitable, if we could invite the witness to take his headphones off, but following what I said yesterday, not to leave Court, I'd be entirely content with him simply to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if we ever meet a similar situation, we might ask prior to deciding -- determining what technique to use, perhaps ask the victims and witness section for advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On which, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially on language knowledge. The question is whether someone --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see. His degree of understanding, Your Honour. Yes, I'm obliged. I'm sorry, I was not understanding it was a language thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a bit short, perhaps. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So may I invite the witness to -- or would Your Honour please invite the witness to take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you take your headphones off, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Simply to say this, and this is not intended to initiate some enormous great debate or submission or motion this afternoon, but Your Honour the Defence do not feel ready for this witness. But I'm not asking for an adjournment this afternoon in order not to proceed to cross-examine him, but the basis is this, Your Honour: We do not feel ready in the sense that we, and this does in fact apply to every member of the team, we do not feel, and I don't want to reargue the matter before Your Honour, but I must state what the position is now in relation to each witness and each specific witness, we do not feel that we have had, in relation to this witness, adequate time to consider the relevant material and to sift the relevant material and to read such material as one would wish to read in order to decide what's relevant, what isn't relevant, simply to explore the material. And I entirely endorse and accept comments and implications that Your Honour has made. Of course, it's not real life that Defence counsel or anybody reads every line of every document. That simply isn't the real world, and that would be wasteful, and this team, we hope, is as experienced as any other team and is able to form sometimes quite robust judgements about what needs to be looked at and what doesn't need to be looked at. This is not a perfect world, and we do frequently and normally make those judgements, and of course we are very used to making them in our professional life over many, many years. But we are put in a position to having to make those judgements in circumstances often where it's not the judgement we would make. We simply cannot absorb the amount of material in the time available. And Your Honour, I do wish to stress that we have -- we are working just about all the time, and I've already said that we are working beyond any sustainable level. It's only because we have been brought into court for the very last week before the recess that what we are doing this week is possible at all because Your Honour, with respect I would not permit my team to sustain this level of work for week in and week out. It is simply impossible. But the position is this, Your Honour, the effects of not having sufficient time are not identifiable in the sense that almost by definition we cannot say, therefore, that there is important material or there is relevant material that we have not looked at because ex hypothesi, some of the stuff we have not been able to look at properly. So we can't say that. So the position, Your Honour, is that I do feel equipped to cross-examine this witness on the main areas which I would regard as appropriate for cross-examination, but the risk, and this is where in the sense I want to put down, I hope it comes across in translation, we would say put down a marker, but to record the position very clearly is that while, of course, it is always the position that an application can be made subsequently to a Trial Chamber for a witness to be recalled after his evidence has otherwise been concluded, generally speaking, of course a pretty high threshold has to be met, and there has to be a solid explanation of why that is suggested to be necessary, with identification of why it is that the points from which it is required to recall the witness were points which could not have been dealt with first time round. And Your Honour, it is only if, of course -- naturally it's only if subsequently we come to the conclusion that are sufficiently sufficient areas which have not been covered that we would ever make such an application. But we would wish to make it clear, Your Honour, that in the particular circumstances of this case, part of the foundation of that application, if it were necessary, if there were significant matters, would be that we simply do not have the normal time available to avoid that difficulty first time round. So that's what we wish to place very clearly and firmly on the record, Your Honour, because it would not -- we see that as a reasonable balance because it wouldn't, looking at the other direction, it wouldn't be responsible of us to seek an adjournment in case that should arise because it might not. And that would be very wasteful if we were to make that application. But on the other hand, we distinctly would not wish it to be thought, and we would to substantiate this, I won't waste the Court's time in going into the painful details now, Your Honour. But if that did come about, then of course, the Court, the Trial Chamber might require more information, more details about why it was we felt we did not have sufficient time and what the volume of material was and what the time available was. I wish to place that firmly on the record, Your Honour. And on that footing, to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, having put this on the record, then at least you avoid that if you would later file any motion or submissions or request for recall of this witness, at least you'll not be confronted with the fact that you didn't pay attention to it at the time you cross-examined the witness. That's point one. The other observation I'd like to make, and not as a beginning of a debate, is that the Chamber at least is aware that the Municipality of Kljuc was the one on which it was provisionally reported that there was almost a 95 per cent agreement on important facts. So therefore, it's at least better to have Kljuc at this moment before the recess than any other municipality. You may start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I will reserve any response to that point for the future occasion if it ever arises, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I wonder if you could be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now, he should put his headphones on again. Otherwise he might miss some of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish my questions to be wasted for that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond reason, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, could you be given, please, Exhibit 251, P251 I'm talking about, of course. Now, we looked at this in the course of your evidence earlier today, and we looked at a passage later on. It's on page 6 of the English version. From memory, I think it was page 8 of the B/C/S version. But that's perhaps not critical, section VI, the course of armed operations. But I wish to go back to the -- near the beginning of this document, Mr. Egrlic. On the first page, there's an introductory note. I'm not going to trouble you about the introductory note. Do you then see a heading, "Fundamental causes that have contributed to the deteriorating security situation." Do you see that? It's main heading number two.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And under that heading, number 2, "Position on mobilisation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then of course, Mr. Egrlic, this won't be in dispute at all between us, the presentation of this document is from a particular point of view, so the third line comes across in English: "The games vis-a-vis the justification and legality of mobilisation in the municipality began with the first call-up at the end of June 1991. From September 1991, the Muslim population completely stopped responding to the call-up into JNA units." Mr. Egrlic, just to get this clear, you have in your evidence dealt with and referred to the unwillingness of Bosniaks to respond to the mobilisation call. Do you accept that that was for citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a form of unlawful civil disobedience?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it not the position that under the law of the state of which you were a citizen and of which Bosnia and Herzegovina was part, it was a breach of the law to fail to respond to a mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time that the JNA was a multiethnic army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is your answer to my question "yes," that you agree that it was a form of unlawful civil disobedience?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the earlier period. That would have been a case of civil disobedience when the Presidency of Yugoslavia was the commander of the armed forces and when the army was a multiethnic army. But after the war broke out in Slovenia and subsequently in Croatia, the Presidency of Yugoslavia lost control. It was no longer the supreme commander. The army was then an army that was composed of one ethnic group. And other peoples could not find a place within that army. That was also the case for the Bosniaks from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What, in your view, in 1991 was the status of the Croatian war? Was it a war between two states? Was it a civil war? Or did it involve an insurrection? Or how else did you regard it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it was a war against the secession of Croatia from the Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And wasn't it your understanding that the state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was entitled to take military action to prevent such secession?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have had the right to do that if the conditions had been normal and if all the peoples had been part of that army and that state, if all the peoples had taken part in this action and if war hadn't broken out in Slovenia. However, when Slovenia became independent, Yugoslavia ceased to function as such. It no longer had command, or rather the Presidency no longer had command over the armed forces. The armed forces became a formation composed of Serbs alone. And that is my opinion of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is this right, Mr. Egrlic: Bosniaks refused to respond to mobilisation with the result that the army became monoethnic, and the monoethnicity of the army was the reason for the Bosniaks not responding to mobilisation. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniaks didn't respond to the mobilisation call-up because they didn't want to go to the battlefields in Croatia and to take sides with anyone in that war since it was obvious that certain national problems as far as the Serbs and Croats are concerned hadn't been resolved. This is the reason for which mobilisation was not accepted, because the policies conducted and the political leadership, the policies as a whole with regard to Bosniaks were such that the relationships within Yugoslavia should be established through agreement and not by conducting a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is it fair to paraphrase what you've said as that this was a war between Croats and Serbs which you, Bosniaks, I think is the word we've used mainly throughout your evidence, regarded as "not your war"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniaks thought that war was not a way to resolve the problems that the Croats and Serbs had in the area. And we believed that it wasn't necessary for the Serbian Army to go to Croatia. The Bosniaks believed that it was necessary to find a peaceful solution to the relationships between the republics that had previously constituted Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, by the second half of 1991, there simply was a war, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a war in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. First of all, volunteers, Serbs, went there from Bosnia and Herzegovina and from Serbia. Later on, there were units that were mobilised, too. So there was a war in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Egrlic, is that rather than avoid the question by appealing to the perfectly natural wish for a peaceful solution, once a war had started, then the position was that you simply regarded it, Bosniaks, as "not your war"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position was that no one needed a war. We didn't need it, and no one else needed a war. The position was that problems should be resolved via peaceful means. It's not just that this wasn't our war; it shouldn't have been anyone's war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it your war in your view?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't our war, it wasn't anyone's war. Nothing has ever been solved by conducting a war. That was the position of the Bosniak politicians. It was believed that it wasn't necessary to go to the battlefield in Croatia and fight a war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, did the Serb community in your part of Bosnia and Herzegovina regard the Croatian war as at least "their" war?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the action taken and the fact that volunteers were first sent off and then units were mobilised, on this basis, one could conclude that they believed that it was necessary to get involved in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were there, Mr. Egrlic. Was it your observation that the Serb community where you lived certainly regarded the Croatian war as "their war"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they thought it necessary to help the Serbs in Croatia, and that's why they went there. Whether they thought of that war as theirs or not is a difficult question to answer. But judging by the trouble they took and the fact that they went to fight in Croatia, obviously they thought it necessary to wage that war. Whether a war can be something that can be appropriated as one's own is arguable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, it was bitterly resented, wasn't it, by the Serb community where you lived in 1991 that the Muslims, Bosniaks, clearly and quite deliberately wished to avoid taking part in that war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs believed, as I have already said once, that the failure to respond to mobilisation calls on the part of Bosniaks amounted to their siding with Croats, which was not true. It was a result of the developments I had already described and their belief that war would not lead to anything, that instead it was necessary to reach an agreement on the future of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Their attitude was the well-known one, Mr. Egrlic, wasn't it, during a war, that who is not for us is against us? That was their attitude, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way they acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Egrlic, you have described peaceful relations over a long period in your community, and what we have just been considering and the fundamentally different reaction and attitude towards the Croatian war as between the Serb community and the Bosniak community effectively shattered those good relations, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did lead to their deterioration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you -- Mr. Egrlic, I take it you do your regard yourself to some considerable degree as having been a political animal, a political person in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sir, you may have answered so softly, Mr. Egrlic, it wasn't picked up. I thought I heard you.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you have a general interest in politics which caused you to attempt to follow and to take an intelligent interest in the political currents affecting Yugoslavia and its various constituent parts?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as politics was concerned, I was at the level of municipal authorities, and I did not have a political education or qualifications that would enable me to act as a politician on a larger scale, especially on pan-Yugoslav issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So although you were an active local politician, your own focus and your own interest was on your locality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- is this right, then: You only concerned yourself with any wider pictures so far as it had an impact on your locality where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I just did. Do you agree, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we look back at the document, please, in front of you. Under the heading "war operations," do you see that? It's number III, item III -- it's under the main heading "Fundamental causes that have contributed to the deteriorating security situation" and then in English, of course, it's "War operations," item III. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It says: "The standpoints" -- and the document has talked about mobilisation. We looked briefly at that a few minutes ago. "The standpoints became completely polarised when the issues of attacks on the Serbs and the defence of the Serbian People on the territory of Croatia as well as provocation in the Bosanska Krajina basin of the River Sava were raised. A considerable number of Serbian nationals became volunteers. We also established through intelligence that some Muslim nationals actively took part in enemy formations of the Republic of Croatia." Now, "enemy formations" is clearly talking about Croats, Mr. Egrlic. There can't be any doubt about that. Do you have any knowledge about whether or not that last point, that "some Muslim nationals actively took part in Croat enemy formations" is true?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Egrlic, my question - and I'm being careful about the question -- well, I'm trying to be careful, so I would invite you please to be careful to listen to them and answer them. My first question is whether you have any knowledge as to whether that is or is not true.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this last assertion, if that's what the question refers to, it is not true to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you know something about it, do you, Mr. Egrlic, which gives some weight or value to your own view?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information to the effect that in the former Croatia, there was a certain number Bosniaks working from Kljuc Municipality, Bosniaks who happened to be there when the war started. And I don't rule out the possibility that a number of them had been mobilised and thus found themselves in the ranks of the Croatian Army. But to say that there were Bosniak volunteers from Kljuc Municipality who took up arms and went to Croatia to fight would absolutely not be true. That's my assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we stick to what's in the document, Mr. Egrlic, rather than you raising your own questions which you then go on to answer. The -- if I understand it, you were saying that the proposition here that some Muslim nationals actively took part in enemy formations of the Republic of Croatia is true?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was possible that a number of people who had been working in the territory of Croatia took part. It's possible that they were mobilised by the Croatian Army and participated in that way. As for Bosniak volunteers, or mobilised Bosniaks, there were certainly none in the Croatian theatre of war. If the Bosniaks who worked in Croatia were subject to the obligatory military service, if they were conscripts, then it's possible they were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there was -- well, first of all, Mr. Egrlic, are you saying that you simply don't know anything about that, that it's possible, or that you do, in fact, know something about conscripts who worked in Croatia becoming soldiers in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it. Those are just my assumptions that maybe if they happened to be there anyway, it was one of the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said in an earlier answer: "I have information to the effect that in the former Croatia, there was a certain number of Bosniaks working from Kljuc Municipality, Bosniaks who happened to be there when the war started." And you say, "I don't rule out the possibility." Now, Mr. Egrlic, I don't want to be unfair. You're talking about information that there were a number of Bosniaks working in Croatia but that wasn't a mystery, was it? Let's start from the beginning. It was perfectly obvious, a perfectly well-known fact that there were Bosniaks working in Croatia? Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked there. But please, it's not the same thing to work and to wage war. I already answered. You needn't ask the same question a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond thousand times. I said there were Bosniaks working in Croatia. There is a possibility of which I know nothing actually that they were mobilised and took part in that theatre of war. As for Bosniaks in the Municipality of Kljuc, none were mobilised and there were no volunteers who were sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's submission that the witness is completely correct. This matter has been asked and answered, if the Defence could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I invite the Prosecution to indicate what it is that has been asked and what it is that's been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your first question was whether the witness has any knowledge. The witness has by now answered the question that he had no knowledge. You then confronted him with his answer where he said that he had information, not that -- let me just check that. In my memory, it was not only that Bosniaks were living and working in Croatia, but even Bosniaks from Kljuc, if I'm well informed. And then he at the beginning said he didn't rule out that they might have participated in Croatian units. I do agree with the Prosecution that the question has been put in different forms to the witness a couple of times, and unless you have a new question on the subject, that the matter has been dealt with sufficiently. So I'm not saying that you couldn't ask any questions about the subject any more, but until now this question is whether he had any knowledge; and the second, whether it was true what he said here what has been put to him a couple of times. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you're talking about information you had about people working in Croatia, do we take it you weren't talking about any special information that you had, but it was simply a well-known fact? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
